episodes.title: Chrome Website Notifications Won't Stop? Fix the Permission #Shorts
source_linked_claims: Chrome sites can send notifications; settings and blockers are documented
scenes: Those endless notification popups may be coming from a site you allowed in Chrome. You can revoke that permission.
A noisy notification by itself does not prove your computer is infected. First check which website received permission.
On desktop Chrome, open Settings, Privacy and security, Site settings, then Notifications. Your version may label menus differently.
Find the unwanted site under allowed notifications and block it. Use quieter notification prompts if interruptions continue.
The fix is permission control, not clicking scary alerts. Confirm the site is no longer allowed to notify you.

episodes.title: Your Google Account Still Trusts Old Apps? Check This #Shorts
source_linked_claims: Google Account third-party app and service access management
scenes: That old app you stopped using might still be connected to your Google Account. Review access rather than guessing.
Third-party connections can be used for Sign in with Google or to access permitted account data, depending on your grant.
From your Google Account's security and connections area, review third-party apps and services with access.
If an app no longer needs access, remove its connection. Google documents that access can be revoked.
Removing access stops future access through that grant; it may not erase data already shared with the service.

episodes.title: Five Browser Permissions Worth Checking Before You Click Allow
source_linked_claims: Google Chrome notification and permission controls, Google third party connections
scenes: A fictional website sends notification after notification, even when its tab is closed. You may think it is a virus, but the first useful check is whether the browser has permission to send those alerts.

Websites request specific capabilities and browsers keep rules for them. Some are useful during a task; others outlive the reason you granted access. This tutorial shows a review workflow using original illustrative settings screens.

On desktop Chrome, open Settings, Privacy and security, Site settings, then Notifications. Look for unfamiliar websites in the allowed list. Block those you no longer want to hear from instead of engaging with suspicious notification content.

Location requests may make sense for maps or local search, but not every website needs the same access. In Chrome Site settings review location grants and remove those you do not recognize or no longer need.
A video meeting may need camera permission. A random page usually does not. Review which websites have camera access, and keep only the sites that currently require it.

Microphone permission can be appropriate for online calls. If an unfamiliar website has retained that grant, review it. Deny unneeded access and allow a trusted site again when an actual task requires it.

Web notifications and popup windows are separate settings. Turning off popup windows does not necessarily revoke a website's previously granted notification permission. Check the specific control tied to the symptom.
Chrome provides a quieter notification-request experience. This changes how permission prompts appear; it does not magically delete every grant you previously gave. Review allowed sites first.

Browser site permissions are not the same as connections to a Google Account. Separate account access can persist through an app or service. Visit your official account settings to review third-party connections independently.
If a connected app is no longer useful, remove its access through official account controls. Remember that revoking access does not prove data already provided to that service has been deleted.
A notification saying your computer is infected is not a reliable diagnosis. Avoid clicking alarming links to fix the issue. Open Chrome settings directly and inspect permission grants yourself.

Finish with a quick audit: notification sites, location grants, camera, microphone, and unrelated third-party account connections. Remove only permissions you do not need and verify trusted services still work.
